Where it began

Eoin Morgan was born in Dublin on 10 September 1986 and raised in Rush, where he learned the game at the local cricket club. As a teenager he also played hurling twice a week, and he reckoned the one thing it gave his batting was the grip for the reverse sweep. His school won three Leinster Senior Schools Cup titles with him in the team, and a short stay at Dulwich College in London was where the idea of playing for England took hold.

He came up through every Irish youth side, became Ireland's youngest senior international and captained them at the 2006 Under-19 World Cup. His runs across his Under-19 World Cups came to 606.

The player

His one-day debut for Ireland, against Scotland in 2006, ended in a run-out on 99, the first time anyone had fallen there on ODI debut. In Abu Dhabi early in 2007 his 209 not out against the UAE was the first first-class double hundred for Ireland. At Middlesex, standing in as captain at just 22, he led the county to a Championship win over Kent.

England picked him in 2009, and his Test debut followed at Lord's against Bangladesh in May 2010. That summer he made a hundred against Pakistan at Trent Bridge, and in 2011 he added another as England piled up 710 for 7 against India on the way to becoming the top-ranked Test side. He played 16 Tests, all by 2012, scoring 700 runs at 30.43 with two hundreds, a best of 130, and holding 11 catches. A hard tour of the UAE in early 2012, when Pakistan's spinners troubled all of England's batsmen, proved to be his last in Tests.

What made him special

In the shorter forms he was something else again, inventive and aggressive. He won the World Twenty20 with England in 2010, and was the first man to make one-day hundreds for two countries. Made England's one-day captain just before the 2015 World Cup, he set about changing how the side played once that tournament was over. Four years later, at Old Trafford, he struck 17 sixes in an innings of 148 against Afghanistan, then a record. On 14 July 2019 his team beat New Zealand on boundary count, after both the final and the super over had finished level, to win England's first World Cup.

Away from the middle

He was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year, and the 2020 New Year Honours made him a CBE. MCC made him an Honorary Life Member in 2023. He stepped away from international cricket in June 2022 and from playing altogether in February 2023, and moved into commentary. As of 2026 no one had played more one-day internationals for England.

And finally

His first time on the field in a Lord's Test came in 2007, as England's twelfth man, standing in for Matthew Hoggard. Three years later he was back at Lord's for his own Test debut, and this time he got to bat.
